booklets/brochures for the management of the coconut mite. 
(iii) The Coconut Development Board is extending assistance for 
training the coconut growers. 
(iv) The Project Directorate of Biological Control (ICAR), 
Bangalore has developed a bio-pesticide Mycohit based on a 
fungus "Hirsutella thompsoni' for large scale field trials 
against the coconut mite. 
(v) Biopesticide solumam based on neem preparation has been 
registered under section 93(B) of the Insecticides Act, 1968 
for the control of Coconut mit.

(a) whether it is a fact that the growth rate of production of 
foodgrains has dropped to 1.8 per cent in the 1990s from 3.54 per cent in 
the 1980s as pointed out in the mid-term appraisal report of the 
Planning Commission; 
(b) if so, die reasons for this decleration and has any study been 
made;

commodities; and

(e) what are proposed reforms during the next year? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) to (e) Yes, Sir. 
There has been decleration in the growth rate of foodgrains production 
during the decade of 90s compared to 80s mainly due to diversion of 
cropped area to more remunerative commercial crops and plateauing of 
yield rates in high productivity areas. 
To increase the production and productivity and thus growth rate, 
various steps have been taken by the Government. These include, 
inter-alia, implementation of centrally sp onsored integrated Cereal 
Development Programmes in Rice/Wheat/Coarse Cereals Based 
Cropping System areas. National Pulses Development Project, National 
Oilseeds Production Programme and Seed Minikit Scheme. Under these 
programmes/projects, incentives are provided to farmers for use of 
high yielding varieties of seeds, application of integrated pest 
management propagation of scien tific water management including 
micro irrigation and improved farm implements. In addition, Field 
demonstration on farmers' holding including training of farmers and 
farm labourers are organized for ef fective transfer of technology. 
Further, under the National agenda for Governance, the Government has 
set priorities for doubling food production in ten years (1997-98 to 
2007-08), adopting regionally differentiated growth strategies, creation 
of farming infrastructure and more efficient use of resources. These 
strategies will help to increase growth rate of agriculture. Reforms for 
improving overall efficiency and productivity are being undertaken.

CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government had inadequate grain 
storage facilities to stock die foodgr ain produced, as a result of which 
it had to be dumped on the market at lower prices or even lying at 
various locations without proper storage facilities leading to pilferage 
and damage; 
(b) the shortage of storage space and infrastructure has been 
highlighted for many years but no action has been taken; and 
(c) if so, what are Government's views in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI 
SRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) to (c) There is no serious problem for storage 
of foodgrains as the FCI has a total storage capacity of 26.64 million 
tonnes (both owned & hired) against which it had a stock of 22.71 
million tonnes as on October 1, 2000. Further, the State agencies 
procuring on behalf of the FCI or having decentralized procurement 
also have a capacity of about 20 million tonnes (owned & hired). 
There is a plan scheme for construction of godowns under the 
Five Year Plan. The construction of godowns is a continuous process. 
New godowns are constructed every year under this plan scheme 
subject to the allocation of plan funds in a year. Further, Government 
have formulated a National Policy on storage, handling and 
transportation of foodgrains which ai ms at harnessing the resources of 
public and private sectors, bom domestic and foreign, to build and 
operate infrastructure in bulk hand ling, storage and transportation of 
foodgrains in the country. Under this policy, the private sector will 
also be encouraged to build conventional godowns in which they will 
store and maintain foodgrains procured by Government agencies, for 
which they will be entitled to storage charges.

388. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the 
Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Antyodya scheme to provide 
foodgrains to the vast majority of people below the poverty line has 
been turned down by Government; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether he has devised any alternative plan to take care of the 
food demands of the poor and the deprived population in the country; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI 
SRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) and (b) Keeping in view the mounting stock 
of foodgrains with FCI, various steps to increase offtake have been 
considered by the Government. One of the steps under the title. 
"Antyodaya Scheme" envisaged distribution of 25 kg. of foodgrains 
per family per month at highly subsidised prices to 1 crore poorest 
among the BPL families. No decision has been taken on this scheme. 
(c) and (d) In order to ensure availability of foodgrains to the 
families below poverty line, the G overnment of India launched the 
Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) with its focus on the poor 
in June, 1997. Under the scheme, each BPL family was entitled to 10 
kg. of foodgrains per month at specially subsidised prices. Keeping in 
view the consensus on increasing the allocation of foodgrains to BPL 
families, the Government of India increased the allocation to BPL 
families from 10 kg. to 20 kg. of foodgrains per family per month at 50% 
of economic cost from April, 2000. The allocation of foodgrains for 
BPL families has now been determined on the basis of population 
projections of Registrar General as on 01.03.2000 instead of the earlier 
base of projected population of 1995. 
The Government has taken the following decisions for 
distribution of foodgrains to the poor and the deprived at subsidised 
rates: 
1. To allocate foodgrains at BPL rates to State Governments @ 5 
kg. per head per month for covering categories of indigent 
people living in welfare institutions such as beggar homes, 
hostels for SC/ST/ backward class students/homes for 
nariniketans etc. sponsored by 
82

the State Governments and the concerned administrative 
Ministry of Government of India. 
2. To allocate foodgrains under me Annapooma scheme to 
indigent old persons even in the case of those receiving old-age 
pension from the State Governments. 
3. To allocate foodgrains at CIP applicable for BPL families for all 
welfare schemes implemented by the various Ministries of 
Government of India. 
4. To allocate foodgrains at the ra te applicable for BPL families 
to the  State Governments for undertaking "food-for-work" 
programmes in the State, as also for the Greening India 
Campaign. 
5. To allocate foodgrains at BPL rates for development schemes, 
where the beneficiaries belong to the BPL category, 
implemented by NGOs sponsored  by the State Governments 
and the administrative Ministry in Government of India, as also 
by the international organisations like the World Food 
Programmes.

Commerce in the country, the Government has enacted

framework for amongst others recognition of electronic 
contracts, prevention of computer crimes, and electronic 
filing/documents. The mechanis m of digital signature has 
been approved to address the issues of jurisdiction, 
authentication and origination.

circuits, microprocessors, data  display tubes and deflection

recommendations of the Chief Minister Conference held in July, 1996. 
The broad objective of the programme was to ensure that people have 
access to basic services in order to improve their quality of life. 
The seven Basic Services identified for priority attention were: 
1. 100 per cent coverage of provision of safe drinking water in 
rural and urban areas. 
2. 100 per cent coverage of primary health service facilities in 
rural and urban areas. 
3. Universalisation of primary education. 
4. Provision of Public Housing Assistance to all shelterless poor 
families. 
5. Supplementary Nutrition via Extension of Mid-Day Meal 
Programme in primary schools to all rural blocks and urban 
slums and disadvantaged sections and supplementary nutrition 
programme implemented as part of ICDS. 
6. Provision of connectivity to all unconnected villages and 
habitations. 
7. Streamlining of the Public Dist ribution System with a focus 
on the poor. 
THE BMS programme has been discontinued from the year 2000-
01. In its place, Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) has been 
launched from the current year. The PMGY envisages additional central 
assistance for selected services. These arc education, health, shelter, 
drinking water and nutrition. In addition rural roads have been given 
priority under the scheme for which a separate provision of Rs. 2500 
crores has been made in the current year.

categories. These are: (a) self-employment programmes aimed at direct 
income generation for the poor through asset building, bypassing the 
general growth process, and (b) wage employment programmes. Since the 
Sixth Five Year Plan (1980—85), the Government has been implementing 
these programmes. Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) 
has been the major self-employment programme and it has been in 
operation in all the blocks of the country since 1980. The wage 
employment programme initially was National Rural Employment 
Programme (NREP) during the Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh Plan, 
another wage employment programme under the name Rural Labour 
Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP) was introduced. Then in 
1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was launched by merging the National 
Rural Employment Programme and the Rural Labour Employment 
Guarantee Programme, and it beca me the main wage-employment 
programme. In addition, several programmes to help the poor were also in 
operation until March, 1999. These programmes are: Million Wells Scheme 
(MWS), Employment Assurance 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [23 November, 2000] 
Scheme (EAS), Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas 
(DWCRA), Training of Rural Youth for Self-Employment (TRYSEM), 
Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, IRDP and allied programmes, alongwith 
Million Wells Scheme have been restructured into single self-employment 
programme called the Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with 
the primary objectives of focussed approach to poverty alleviation. Jawahar 
Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has also been restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi 
Yojana (JGSY) with the primary objective of creation of demand driven 
community, village infrastructure including durable assets at the village 
level and assets to enable the rural poor to increase the opportunities for 
sustained employment. Its secondary objective is generation of 
supplementary employment for the unemployed poor in the rural areas. 
Employment Assurance Scheme has also been restructured from 1999- 
2000 to make it the single wage employment programme. While the basic 
parameters have been retained, the scheme has become allocative scheme 
instead of demand driven scheme and a fixed annual outlay is to be 
provided to the states. The wage employment under the programme is 
given to Below Poverty Lines (BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swama Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is 
the main poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, 
which has subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation 
programmes, viz., Nehru Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Services for 
the Poor (UBSP) and Prime Minister's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication 
Programme (PMIUPEP), seeks to provide gainful employment to urban 
unemployed or underemployed poor through encouraging the setting up of 
self employment ventures or provision of wage employment. The 
implementation of SJSRY is relying on suitable community structures on 
the UBSP pattern and delivery of inputs under this programme is through 
the medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and such community 
structure.

militants would not take undue advantage of this ceasefire. 
Therefore, our understanding was that the Government had, in 
fact, taken ail possible precautions. What has happened 
yesterday, the killing of innocent truck drivers, I think, is a most 
ghastly incident. It needs to be condemned. It once again, I 
think, reinforces the plea that the Government while it 
negotiates, while it offers not to take the initiative in counter-
insurgency measures, should never, I think, weaken its guard 
against these elements. It appears to me that something has 
been lacking and that is why the militants have taken advantage 
of that weakness to kill the Sikh truck drivers. We condemn that. 
We urge upon the Government that they must ensure adequate 
protection to all our citizens whet her they belong to the minority 
or they belong to the majority. All of our citizens are entitled to 
the protection of the law. It is the bounden duty of the 
Government to ensure safety. We urge upon the Government 
not to lag behind in this regard. The Government have made an 
offer; and, as I said, we welcomed that. But it does not mean 
that if the terrorists strike, we will sit back. If they strike, they 
must be given an appropriate reply, in a befitting manner.   
Thank you.

SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: Therefore, let me go now to

about hot pursuit. We had another Cabinet Minister saying, no

months later, the Prime Minister talked about our 'shared vision 
of peace' and took the bus to Lahore. Then we had the Kargil,

your eminent Members raised this issue. We have the 
ceasefire. Now we have welcomed the ceasefire. Then what is 
the message that you are trying to convey through this 
ceasefire? According to me, you are trying to convey the 
message that we have now harmonised relations; we must 
open the gate for a political solution. If that is the message, why 
have you prevented the cricket team from going to Pakistan? 
This is something which would cause no harm at all. The cricket 
team going to Pakistan would strengthen peoples- to- people 
relations. There is no consistency in your policy towards 
Pakistan. Your policy swings from extreme to extreme, and 
therefore, as far as Pakistan is concerned, what is required is 
quiet diplomacy at official level and loud dialogue like the cricket 
team visiting at the people- to- people level. I will conclude by 
saying that the paramount objectives of our foreign policy 
remain the pursuit of development and the preservation of 
national sovereignty. Let us not lose sight of that and the 
important changes that have been made. I did not take more 
than ten minutes, Sir. Thank you.

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, 
the Hon. Foreign Minister has very eloquently enunciated the 
requisite qualities of a very good foreign policy, but, Sir, I would 
also say that we should have an introspection as to whether our 
policy does possess all those qualities. In my opinion, a foreign 
policy has to be very pragmatic. It should not be dictated by 
political considerations. It should have some long-term interest 
as its objective. There should be no ad hocism in formulating a 
foreign policy. It is true that the growing importance of our 
country is being felt by the comity of nations at the international 
level. We have been claiming that we are non-aligned. But I 
have got my own reservations, to what extent our country is 
non-aligned. We have been aligned with Russia for several 
years, but, now, there seems to be a tilt. 
I am not accusing anyone. I am a man who advocates 
that a foreign policy should be very pragmatic. It should 
subserve the national interests, it should subserve the economic 
interests of the country and it should be in a position to preserve 
and protect the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the nation; 
I do admit. Sir, I have read the statements of both the Foreign 
Minister and the Home Minister. The Foreign Minister has said 
that they do not have good relations with Israel because of local 
vote banks--l have read it in the newspapers-, but the Home 
Minister has gone to the extent of admitting or considering that 
we can have a military understanding also. Sir, to what extent it 
is beneficial to our national interests and what its ramifications 
will be, it is time for us to introspect. It has got certain aspects. It 
has a human aspect. Sir, millions of people are working in the 
Gulf countries. Expatriats are there, and our country's interests 
are there. The Middle East is a very good market for Indian 
products and it has got a tremendous oil potentiality which is 
totally devastating our economy. The entire economy is being 
affected by the hike in oil prices. Added to this, we have got 
Muslim fraternity here. The present scenario is, no day passes 
when the price of one product or the other is not hiked. Sir, in 
this scenario, see the statements or the pronouncements that 
have been made by the Ministers of our country. Are these not 
deterimental to our national interests? 
As far as military cooperation with Israel is concerned, if 
what I read in the newspapers is correct, I advise the 
Government to be cautious. Ultimately, it is an ally of the United 
States.   After all, we could not get our 
248 

[23 November, 2000J RAJYA SABHA 
helicopter services to Great Britain because that happens to be 
a friend of the United States! 
Today, Pakistan has been making a lot of insinuations 
against this country and General Musharraf is trying to compare 
the Israeli-Palestinian issue with the Indo-Pakistan issue on 
Kashmir. Recently, at the meeting of the Organisation of Islamic 
Conference in Doha or somewhere-l don't remember the exact 
name—he has mentioned this. My sincere advice to the 
Government is that we should be cautious in dealing with Israel. 
Let us not face a Waterloo in the Middle East. It is going to be 
very costly for the nation. Our Foreign Policy should be a non-
partisan affair. Otherwise, our country's Foreign Policy will lose 
its proper perspective. It should not be a party affair. I advise 
the Government to have friendly relations with our neighbours. 
If the European countries, numbering 15, could form a 
confederation, the European Union, why can't we form such a 
confederation along with our neighbours? Why can't we 
explore,such a possibility? I fully concur with the views 
expressed by the earlier speaker. It seems that he has got very 
good knowledge about the foreign affairs since he had served in 
the Ministry of External Affairs as Minister of State. It is simply 
like a pendulum, going from one extreme to another extreme. 
I will discuss about two or three countries who are our 
neighbours. Take, for example, Nepal. It is very close to China. 
It is another Hindu country. But it is very close to China. If you 
go to Nepal, you can see all the products made in China. Their 
products are dumped in Nepal. It is not the case with our 
country. Our products are not dumped there. Our products are 
not available in Nepal. A lot of refugees from Bhutan are staying 
there. My advice to the Government is to play a constructive 
role and bring them together. Bhutan is ruled by a king and the 
people there want democracy. The people are driven out of that 
country and they are taking shelter in Nepal. Our neighbours 
should be stable politically. Then only can we have peace 
around our country. We have to take an initiative in that 
direction and try to bring both the parties together and solve the 
problem. 
Now, take, for example, Bangladesh. We should have 
closer economic ties with Bangladesh. Bangladesh was virtually 
bifurcated from Pakistan and made a nation at the insurance of 
our country. In November, 1971, we took a lot of pain and we 
incurred a huge expenditure. We declared war against 
Pakistan, bifurcated it and created Bangladesh. But, in spite of 
that, we don't have good relations with Bangladesh.   The 
political

Suicides due to depression 
* 85. SHRI DINA NATH MISHRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to slate: 
(a) whether 10 to 20 million people are suffering from mental illness due 
to lack of awareness and proper (real men I and about half of them commit 
suicide, as reported in The Statesman dated 17th October, 2000; 
(b) whether sixty per cent suicides arc due to depression; 
(c) if so, whether Government propose to identify sections suffering 
from psychological disorders and provide them proper treatment; 
(d) whether some NGOs are working in this field; and 
(e) if so, what success has been achieved so Tar in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Epidemiological studies have revealed that 1 to 2% 
of the population have major mental disorders and 5 to 10% suffer from 
minor mental disorders. However, it is not true that half of all the people 
suffering from various mental illnesses commit suicide. In fact, the total 
number of suicides reported in the country as per information available with 
the National Crime Records Bureau for the year 1998 is 104713 only. 
Suicides are commonly associated with depressive disorders, and all 
the persons afflicted with mental di sorders may not be suffering from 
depressive disorders. However, th ere is widespread ignorance about 
various aspects of mental disorders and about the fact that appropriate 
treatment is available for mentally ill patients. 
It- is also not true that 60% of suicides are due to depressive disorders. 
Studies on suicides conducted in different centres in India show that a 
variety 
22 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of psychological, social, economic and personal factors are responsible 
for suicides. Many persons committing suicide may also be suffering 
from long standing painful or untreatable physical conditions. 
The Government has already initiated a pilot programme of providing 
care for persons with mental disorders in selected districts in the country. the 
District Mental Health Programme is currently being implemented in 22 
districts in 20 States and Union Territories. Its aim is to identify persons 
suffering from serious mental disorders and epilepsy and manage them at 
the primary health care centre and district level by trained doctors and with 
the active support of the families and the community in which the patient 
lives. 
A growing number of Non Govern mental Organizations [NGOs] 
have .recently started showing interest in the field of mental health care as 
well as suicide prevention. Some of the prominent NGOs are the Medico 
Pastoral Association in Bangalore. SNEHA — A suicide prevention 
programme in Chennai, Richmond Fellowship India in Bangalore and 
New Delhi, SCARF in Chennai. San jivini in Delhi and Samaritans in 
Calcutta. NGOs work to increase public awareness about mental illnesses, 
decrease stigma related to mental disorders. Provide rehabilitation 
services to mentally ill, provide residential care and facilities for chronic 
mentally ill, run counselling and walk-in services for persons with minor 
mental disorders, crisis intervention service, etc.

has been/is proposed to be initiated; and

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. CR 
THAKUR): (a) to (d) Kala-Azar is endemic in the States of Bihar and West 
Bengal and sporadic cases are recorded in Uttar Pradesh. There has been a 
steady decrease in number of cases in the endemic States. 
The Kala-Azar Control Programme is in operation as a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme since 1990-91. Government of India is supplying anti-Kala-Azar drugs 
and insecticides to the affected States. Funds are also provided for IEC, training 
and organising campaigns. The state Governments bear the entire operational 
costs for spraying insecticides and are responsible for implementation of the 
programme. 
The programme has resulted in overall decline of 83.5 per cent in incidence 
and 80% in recorded deaths due to Kala-Azar in 1999 as compared to peak 
registration in 1992. To further strengthen the efforts against Kala-Azar. 
Government of India has constituted an Expert Committee to review the 
programme and to suggest a focussed strategy for elimination of the disease.

568. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: 
SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY: 
Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact (hat at the State Health Ministers' Conference 
in September, 2000, it was agreed with the con (en (ion of medical 
scientists that (he ban on non-iodised sal( be continued; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that several medical experts wanted the 
ban against non-iodised salt to continue as any move to withdraw (he 
same could be a national disaster; 
 
(c) whether UNICEF has also expressed concern over Government's 
decision to lift ban on consumption on non-iodised salt; 
(d) if so. the details thereof; and 
(e) what steps the Ministry would take to honour the sentiments 
expressed by various organizations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) In the 
meeting convened in September, the Slate Health Ministers expressed 
their views on the central notification issued on 10.5.2000 which 
proposed to remove (he res(ric(ion on sale of iodised salt for direct 
human consumption. 
Medical opinion is divided about whether it is appropriate to make 
consumption of iodised salt compulsory to combat Iodine Deficiency 
Disorders. There are many segments of the population, including 
medical experts, who do not support the use of compulsion in matters 
relating to public health, and who advocate the need to promote 
awareness, availability and accessibility of iodised salt. 
(c) and (d) UNICEF has expressed concern over the lifting of the 
Central notification restricting the sale of non-iodised salt for direct 
human consumption. 
90 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) The restriction on sale of non-iodised salt was finally removed to 
provide for a system that allows adequate flexibility to accommodate 
those who believe that there should be no compulsion in matters 
relating to public health, and that the use of iodised salt to combat IDD 
should ideally be promoted through creation of greater awareness, by 
monitoring the accessibility, availability and affordability of this 
product. 
The need for a statutory compulsi on for sale of iodised salt is 
contingent upon the local social conditions, dietary habits and slate of 
the economy. This aspect is best judged by the State Governments who 
are belter aware of local conditions and who can enforce the ban in 
such areas where the need is percieved. It was felt by the Central 
Government that the decision whether or not to place a ban on sale of 
non-iodised salt, and if yes,, in which areas should be left to the State 
Governments. Consequent upon that the Central Government withdrew 
its notification in this regard. Similar restriction, however, continues to 
be in force in most States/UTs through notifications issued by them 
under the powers available to States in this regard. 
Compulsory iodisation is not th e sole strategy available for 
promoting the use of iodised salt for combating IDD. Creation of 
greater awareness through IEC and increasing availability, 
affordability and accessibility are ke y factors in this regard, and 
Government proposes to focus on th ese aspects to achieve the same 
objective.

Purchase of Locomotives/coaches from German firms 
636. SHRI RAJU PARMAR; 
SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR:  
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to refer to answer to 
Starred Question 294, given in the Rajya Sabha on 11 th August, 2000 
and state: 
154 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) what are the reasons for purchase of locomotives/coaches from abroad 
when these are being manufactured indigenously; and 
(b) what is the price difference between indigenously manufactured 
locomotives/coaches and the ones purchased from German firms? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) The locomotives and coaches running on Indian 
Railways are manufactured with technologies imported in 1950s and 1960s. 
These designs have been stretched to their limits and can no longer sustain the 
present day demands of longer and faster trains. In the meanwhile, technology 
has advanced considerably elsewhere in the world to enable cost effective, 
comfortable and safe operations. The purchase of a small quantity of 
locomotives and coaches from abroad alongwith transfer of technology was 
considered essential to enable our Production Units to manufacture 
state-of-the-art locomotives/coaches indigenously with the latest technology. 
(b) No locomotives have been purchased from German firms. However, 24 
coaches are procured from M/s ALSTOM Linke Hoffman Busch, Germany. 
The price of the imported coach vis-a-vis the indigenous version of same type 
is as shown below: 
   Type of coach     FOB price of Manufacturing cost of old design, 
    imported coach   coach produced at RCF, Kapurthala 
AC Chair Car     Rs. 4.62 crores Rs. 64.48 lakhs 
  Generator Van    Rs. 4.51 crores        Rs. 101.67 lakhs 
These prices are, however, not readily comparable due to the following 
reasons: 
1. The price of the imported coach in cludes costs of engineering and 
development, amortised over a small batch of 24 coaches. 
2. The imported coaches are of state-of-the-art technology, whereas the 
coaches currently produced indigenously are of much older design and 
technology. 
3. In view of the economies of scale, cost of production of these coaches to 
the new design, will come down eventually as we take up regular 
manufacture in large numbers in our Production Units.

Freight information system 
† 637.   SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK: 
PROF. RAM GOPAL YADAV: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Railway Board had ever prepared any proposal for 
Freight Information System; if so, when and the details thereof; 
(b) the amount spent on the said proposal and the company to 
which the contract for the said work was awarded; 
(c) the present status of the said FIS scheme and the amount of 
losses suffered so far by the Railways in this regard; and 
(d) to whom Government consider responsible for the losses 
suffered or being suffered by the Railways and the action Government 
are contemplating in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Based on the 
decisions taken in the Inter-ministerial meeting of Secretaries in 1981, 
a project was sanctioned to install a computer based Freight 
Operations Information System (FOIS) in 1983-84. In 1983, a 
consultancy contract was awarded to M/s CANAC International of 
Canadian Railway for supply of so ftware called Train Reporting And 
Control System (TRACS). Based on the Detailed Project Document 
^DPD) prepared in 1986 in consultation with the consultants, the 
Planning Commission approved the project in 1989 at an abstract cost 
of Rs. 1098 crore. While the complete project was to include several 
modules for entire Indian Railways, a part estimate was sanctioned for 
Rs. 267 crores for implementation only on Northern Railway. Due to 
inflexibility of TRACS to adapt to changed Indian Railways' 
operational practices, an expert committee of IIT Delhi was appointed in 
1995 to undertake a technical evaluation of the project and make 
recommendations suggesting the course of action to be followed. 
Based on the recommendations of the expert committee, that 
recommended development of prototype of two core modules of the 
project and testing on the test bed before undertaking field 
implementation, the strategy for implementation of FOIS was revised 
in 1998. A partnership with Ministry of Information 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
156 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Technology (MIT) was set up and M/s. CMC Ltd., an undertaking under 
MIT, was awarded a contract for developing the two core modules of the 
FOIS for implementation over the en tire Indian Railways. The total 
expenditure on die project so far is about Rs. 216 crores. In view of 
changed strategy, the revised estimated cost for implementation of two 
core modules on entire Indian Railways is Rs. 426 crores 
approximately. 
(c) One core module for monitoring die movement of rakes has 
already been implemented successfully on the Northern Railway. This is 
likely to be extended over all Indian Railways by March 2001. The 
other core module for management of terminals is likely to be 
implemented by the end of March 2003. There is no financial loss 
suffered lis Railways have gained valuable experience during field trails 
of the imported software which prepared the ground for change in the 
strategy and ultimately led to successful implementation of one core 
module on Northern Railway. 
(d) Does not arise.

647. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of SCIENCE

(a) whether Government have undertaken any review of progress made by

system; and 
(b) if so, what are the findings of such a review? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) and (b)The 
programmes in the area of bio-technology taking note of the advances, 
relating to agriculture and health care system are regularly reviewed by 
high powered expert committees. The Department of Bio-technology 
has a Scientific Advisory Committee with very eminent scientists from 
India; it has a Standing Advisory Committee-Overseas with very 
renowned non-resident Indian scientists from USA and other 
European Countries. There is a Bio-technology Research and 
Promotion Committee under the chairmanship of a an eminent bio-
technologist; there are 17 expert task forces in specific areas e.g. 
Agriculture and Medical Bio-technology. These expert committees 
review the progress of all programmes at least once a year and also 
identify new areas. 
In Agriculture Biotechnology, there have been significant 
achievements. Research on priority crops such as rice, wheat, mustard, 
chickpea/pigeonpea has given promising leads eg.—using tissue 
culture induced variation two mustard varieties "Pusa Jaikishan* and 
"Pusa Bold' have been released and are popular among farmers; also 
transgenic mustard lines showing re sistance to drought and salinity; 
toward hybrid seed production transgenic male sterile lines and fertility 
restorer lines of mustard, and insect resistant transgenics of rice, cabbage 
and tomato have been developed by incorporating Bt genes. A novel 
seed storage protein gene (ArnAl) from Amaranth has been introduced in 
potato in order to improve nutritional quality. Fully regenerating Coker 
310 line of cotton is available, and sysnthesis of modified Cry 1A (c) 
gene is in progress for developing transgenic cotton cultivatrs resistant 
to bollworm. Recently India has joined International Rice Genome 
Sequencing Programme to sequence part of chromosome 11. Apart 
from high-throughout sequencing experience, the project would lead to 
the development of superior rice varieties resistant to pests and diseases. A 
major initiative on biofertilizer and biopesticide development, field trials 
and training of farmers has given rice dividends. The efficacy of 
various biopesticides has been demonstrated in an area of about 
164

60,000 h. covering various important crops, and around 10,000 
farmers have been trained on use of different bio-ferti1isers. 
In the health care area, a number of diagnostic technologies have 
been developed and transferred to the industries for 
commercialisation. Last year 1.4 lakh doses of LEPROVAC, an 
immunomodulator developed at the National Institute of Immunology 
were used by NGOs and private pracu ations for Leprosy control. Two 
vaccines for cholera and rotaviral diarrhoea are undergoing clinical trials 
with encouraging results. A National jai Vigyan Science & Technology 
Mission on Development of New generation Vaccines has been 
initiated for six major diseases viz. Cholera, rabies, malaria, 
tuberculosis, Japanese encephalitis and HIV/AI DS. Certain vaccines 
under this programme are in the advance stage of development. A 
major initiative on genetics, ge nomics and functional genomics has 
given a new insight into disease scenario specially for vaccines and 
diagnostics.

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI NITISH 
KUMAR): Sir, during 1999-2000, the States of Arunachal 
Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan. Tripura, 
Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal were affected by floods 
causing widespread damage to life and property. As per 
available information, the floods, excluding floods due to 
cyclone, resulted in loss of about 900 human lives and 3,900 
cattle besides causing damage to cropped area in 7.45 lakh 
hectares and 8.82 lakh houses. 
This year, several States in the country received heavy 
rainfall during the Southwest monsoon resulting in floods 
causing loss of human life and cattle and loss/damage to 
houses and property. Arunachal Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh 
and Andhra Pradesh had flash floods. The cumulative rainfall 
during 1.6.2000 to 11.10.2000 was excess only in 12 out of 35 
meteorological sub-divisions in the country but still a number of 
States faced floods. 
As per reports received from the States this year, 
Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar. Gujarat, 
Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, 
Punjab, Sikkim, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal faced flood 
situations of varying magnitude. The loss and damage to life 
and property, as reported by these States cumulatively has 
been 2782 human lives, 92,927 cattle, damage to 27.05 lakh 
houses and inundation of the cropped area of 34.48 lakh 
hectares. 
The flood management is primarily the responsibility of 
the States. The State Governments concerned took necessary 
relief measures like payment of ex-gratia to the next of kin of 
the diseased, evacuation of people in the marooned areas, 
despatch of medical teams, opening of relief camps to provide 
shelter to the affected people, air-dropping of food packets, 
opening of veterinary centres, supply of relief materials to the 
affected population, restoration of damaged roads and power 
lines on priority. 
The Government of India was in constant touch with 
the affected States and rendered necessary help. The Army 
and Air Force assisted the State Governments in relief 
measures like evacuation of people, air-dropping of food 
packets and relief materials. Centre's share of Calamity Relief 
Fund. 
183 

RAJYA   SABHA [24 November, 2000] 
CRF, has been released to the States as per the Scheme. The 
Central Teams were deputed to many flood affected States to 
assess the situation and I had also made aerial survey of the 
flood affected areas of the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, 
West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh. My Ministry coordinated the 
Central efforts with various C entral Ministries/Departments for 
providing relief to the affected people. Foodgrains at the BPL 
rates have been supplied to the State Governments particularly 
to the State of Bihar and West Bengal. Medicines, 
disinfectants, bleaching powder, halogen tablets, etc., were 
also sent to the affected States. 
As you may be aware, 75% of the annual rainfall is 
received during south-west monsoon period, from 1st June to 
30thSeptember, itself resulting in heavy rains and floods in 
many parts of the country, causing damage to life and property 
every year. The flood prone areas are Andhra Pradesh, 
Assam. Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya 
Pradesh, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The 
perennial States in regard to regular floods are Assam, North 
Bihar and Eastern parts of Uttar Pradesh. Central Water 
Commission in the Ministry of Water Resources is concerned 
with flood forecasting. India Meteorological Department 
provides necessary support th rough its Flood Meteorological 
Offices. They cater to the requirements of flood forecasting in 
different river catchment areas. FMOs provide Quantitative 
Precipitation Forecast in respect of catchment areas of 
important river to the CWC. Flood forecasting enables 
forewarning about impending flood, to what extent and for how 
long, so that necessary preparatory steps could be taken in 
time. The flood forecasting network consists of 157 stations 
situated in 11 States. 
Flood proofing measures help greatly in the mitigation 
of distress and provide immediate relief to the population in 
flood prone areas. It is essentially a combination of structural 
change and emergency action, not involving any evacuation. 
The techniques adopted consist of providing raised platforms 
for flood shelter for men and cattle and raising the public utility 
installation above flood levels. The progress achieved in flood 
control works as a result of various measures taken is that 
162,000 Km. length of embankments and 32,003 Km. length of 
drainage channel were constructed, 906 towns were protected 
and 4721 villages protected. 
Monitoring  of floods  is also done by remote sensing 
through satellites  which   is  one  of  the  effective  tools  to  
monitor  floods  and  assessment  of flood  damages  in  terms 
of area  inundated,  crop  area  submerged and villages 
marooned.

support the sentiments expressed by the hon. Members in 
regard to the plight of people who are affected by the havoc 
caused by floods in various parts of the country. The people of 
West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh. Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and 
Kerala are the worst affected. Sir, this is an annual feature in 
our country. India is a vast country. If one-year floods affect the 
southern part, the next year it affects the western part, the third 
year it affects the eastern part and the fourth year it affects the 
northern part. So. at least, one part of the country is affected 
every year.  We ftave to save the people

from this havoc caused by floods or drought. We are 
discussing the flood situation in various parts of the country. I 
really feel that West Bengal is the worst affected State. The 
statement of the hon. Minister itself reveals as to how much 
damage has been caused in West Bengal. We must extend our 
full support to the people of West Bengal and also to the 
people of other States who are affected by floods. Sir, this 
havoc caused by floods should be treated as a national 
calamity, not as a responsibility of the State. That is my view. I 
appeal fo the hon. Minister to treat this flood situation as a 
national calamity. Two years back, we experienced the same 
situation in Orissa. This year it has happened in West Bengal, 
Andhra Pradesh and other places. Some areas are affected 
mildly. Mostly the agriculturalists are affected. Their crops have 
got destroyed. The whole irrigation system has got disturbed. 
Tanks and channels have been disrupted. We have noted 
some breaches also. To set right all these things, it will take 
one or two years. The life of  agriculturists and people who are 
affected by floods becomes normal only after one or two years. 
It is very difficult to recoup the position. I would request the 
Central Government to study the matter in detail and establish 
a permanent Calamity Relief Commission. A group, consisting 
of experts, has to be appointed and they should go and visit the 
affected areas, After studying the problems, they should 
recommend some plans for redeeming the distress of the 
affected people. 
Sir, I wish to bring to the notice of the Government the 
situation prevailing in Tamil Nadu, though Tamil Nadu does not 
figure in the statement. It has been stated that Kerala has been 
affected. Sir, the southern-most part of Tamil Nadu borders with 
Kerala and, therefore, certain parts of Tamil Nadu, namely, 
Kanyakumari, Madurai, Ramnad and Tirunelveli districts are 
affected by the climatic changes in Kerala. The rainfall started 
on the 19 th of this month in al! these places, and it is still 
continuing. Big tanks have been breached; channels have been 
disrupted and the entire system of irrigation has been affected. 
So, I request the Government to consider this matter as a 
matter of national importance. The Eleventh Finance 
Commission has also recommended that the State 
Governments should be assisted by the Centre. It has also 
recommended that the Central Government should review the 
situation in the States. It has also specified the Centre-State 
ratio, saying that the Centre should bear 75 per cent of the 
damages and the State should bear the remaining 25 per cent.    
So. I request the Government to look into the matter and

SHRI R. MARGABANDU (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, since independence, only one committee -- the 
one headed by Shri Kelkar 
200 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA   SABHA 
-- had been constituted to find out the reasons as well as 
solutions, so far as floods in the Ganges were concerned. After 
that, no committee has been constituted for this purpose. Floods 
in India have become a regular phenomenon every year. One or 
the other part of the country is always affected by floods. Of 
course, Andhra Pradesh is affected very seriously. This year, the 
State of West Bengal has also been affected badly. Several parts 
of India have been affected. I do not want to level any charge 
against this Government. But Government after Government has 
not taken care to constitute any high-powered committee 
consisting of experts to examine the behaviour of the rivers and 
the reasons behind the floods. These have to be examined. 
Modern technologies are available. We have to have a scientific 
approach and a comprehensive plan to assess this situation. 
Whenever there are floods, which are shortlived, the Central 
Government gives assistance. But that is not sufficient. That 
assistance is only for a short period. If a family gets devastated 
by floods, it takes five to ten years to come back to normalcy, 
Sometimes, families are destroyed or ruined for ever. So, we 
have to evolve a long-term policy. This Government has to 
consider the constitution of a high-powered committee to find out 
the reasons as well as solutions to the problem of floods. After 
all, it is not difficult for the Government to identify the areas that 
are regularly affected by floods, as well as to devise measures 
that should be taken to control the fl oods. Only then, this 
problem can be solved. Calamities are taken very lightly and in 
a very casual manner. Whenever there are floods, people 
assess the situation through helicopters and so on and estimate 
the damages; and that's all. You have to solve the problem for 
all times to come. I do not think any long-term assistance has 
been given in this regard. I request the Government to lay a 
white paper on this issue. Also, we must have a foolproof flood 
management system and there s hould be a mechanism to 
control the floods. Many a time, floods are caused due to 
desiltation, deforestation and erosion of riverbanks. These are 
the main reasons for the floods. I would like to know whether the 
Government would come forward to save the life and property 
from the havoc caused by floods, especially in West Bengal, 
where the situation is alarming. So far as the State of West 
Bengal is concerned, there is also a report in which it is said that 
the Department of Education in the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development informed that it was not in a position to provide any 
assistance because that Ministry does not administer any 
scheme which provides for repair of school buildings that have 
been damaged due to excessive rains and floods. 
201 

RAJYA  SABHA   [24 November, 2000] 
On the one hand, the houses and school buildings have 
been devastated; on the other, the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development is saying that it has no scheme for 
them, and it would not help. What type of attitude is this? 
Should this type of an attitude be adopted by the Government? 
I, therefore, request the Government that all efforts should be 
made to help these people. The farmers and villagers are 
affected the most by these floods. As compared to rural areas, 
urban areas are not affected much by these floods. So, the 70 
per cent of our population which is residing in villages is 
affected by these floods. These poor people are rendered 
homeless, landless and their crops are devastated by floods. 
The Government should see to it that some effective steps are 
taken in order to save these people from floods. The 
Government should formulate a long-term project so that the 
people are saved from these natural calamities. 
[The Vice-Chairman (Shri Suresh Pachouri) in the Chair.]

SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA (Karnataka): Thank you, 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir. The unprecedented rainfall has caused 
a great havoc all over the country. As stated by the Minister of 
Agriculture, it is particularly severe in West Bengal. Andhra 
Pradesh, Karnataka and some other States. So far as 
Karnataka is concerned, these floods resulted in loss of 152 
human lives. Besides this, roads were damaged very badly; 
bridges were destroyed; public buildings and some 55.000 
houses were damaged; and cropped area in 56,000 hectares 
has also been damaged. The State Government of Karnataka 
has asked the Central Government for further financial 
assistance. But so far, the Government has not released the 
amount. The other important thing to be taken into account is 
the human feelings. At that time, whether it is the Central 
Government or the State Government, they had not anticipated 
that the loss would be of that magnitude and that it would 
cause so much havoc to human lives and property. I must also 
say that officers reach there in the normal course, that is, a 
long time after all this damage is done. What do they do? They 
say, "yes, you have suffered heavy losses, you have lost 
everything; but they do not talk about the relief or the 
compensation. Obviously, they would say ' we have written to 
the Government'. The State Government would say 'we have 
asked for financial assistance from the Central Government.' It 
is only after three or four months that some people would go 
there. Their coming after such a long period, does not serve 
any purpose. They cannot compensate the pain and agony 
which the people there underwent three or four months ago. No 
one can explain the sufferings they underwent four months 
ago. Therefore, this situation has to be considered very 
seriously. We cannot hold the Government responsible for the 
Calamity, which took place. The point to be considered in this 
regard, is we should be prepared to meet such challenges. 
Under the circumstances, the hon. Minister said that flood 
management was primarily the responsibility of the State 
Governments.   He has very rightly said this.

THE PROHIBITION OF SMOKING BILL. 2000 
SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL (Nominated):   
Madam, I move: 
That the Bill to provide for the prohibition of 
smoking of tobacco in any form in places of public 
work or use and in public service vehicles since 
smoking has been found injurious not only to the 
smokers but even more to the non-smokers and 
to make provision therefore and for other matters 
connected therewith, be taken into consideration. 
उपसभापितः ऐसा लगता है िक यह Ģावधान तो है क्यȗिक हवाई जहाज 
मȂ Îमोिंकग मना है, पिÅलक Ãलेसेज मे मना है, पािर्लयामȂट मȂ भी अंदर तो मना ही 
है ।  
SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL: Madam, smoking 
considered as a private problem until yesterday is a public 
hazard today. It has been proved beyond any doubt that 
tobacco smoking is injurious not only for the one who indulges 
in it, but it is also as much, harmful, if not more, for those 
around. Cosmetic measures like advertising "Smoking is 
injurious for health" etc. may have succeeded to an extent in 
the developed countries but    these    have    registered    little    
impact    in    the    developing    and 
259 

RAJYA   SABHA [24 November. 2000]  
underdeveloped countries. With the latest research revealing 
grave danger of passive smoking, it has become imperative to 
take stricter measures to curb this menace in our developing 
society in India. Hence this Bill about which the Government 
too, has already given an indication in reply to an Unstarred 
Question on December 10, 1999, that "the Government is 
examining the feasibility of formulating a comprehensive 
legislation for discouraging use of tobacco smoking." 
According to the Delhi Medical Association findings, 
recently reported in the Press, tobacco will emerge as a major 
killer by 2020.- It is estimated that nearly 3.5 million people 
annually die in the world from smoking-related diseases, of 
which two-thirds die in the developing countries. The World 
Health Organisation has reported that over 150 million children 
in the world die of tobacco-induced diseases, one-third of 
which, under five years, die due to acute respiratory infectious 
tobacco smoke. If the trend continues, tobacco use would kill 
nearly 10 million people every year. As it is, over 10 lakh 
people annually, or 3,000 every day, die on account of smoking 
in India. Several lakh more are disabled by tobacco-related 
diseases. The victims include those non-smokers who often 
remain in the company of smokers. 
The report goes on to say, "Tobacco contains harmful 
substances such as nicotine, carbon monoxide and lar. On 
inhalation, these substances enter the bloodstream affecting 
!he brain and causing heart and other ailments. Nicotine 
increases secretion of chemicals like adrenaline which 
increases the heart rate and blood pressure. Nicotine also 
interferes with the functioning of blood vessels, increasing the 
tendency of blood clots. Other adverse effects are respiratory 
infections, gastric ulcers, pregnancy complications, etc." 
Tobacco intake is a major contributing factor for 
causing cancer. It is reported that about 300 million would be 
afflicted by cancer in the next 25 years and about 200 million 
would die due to the disease. A WHO report says that tobacco 
use is responsible for 90 per cent of lung cancer and over 80 
per cent of chronic bronchitis cases. Also, 20 to 25 per cent of 
coronary heart diseases and stroke are attributed to smoking. 
Scientific data shows that there is unmistakable co-
relation between smoking and infertility. If a person smokes 
more than 20 cigarettes a day, his sperm count, a decisive 
factor in fertility, could drop by 60-70  per  cent.    The  infertility  
risk  is  not  confined  to men  alone. 
260 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA   SABHA 
5.00 P.M. 
Women too run the risk of impaired fertility. It also reduces the 
chances of embryo implant. In pregnant women it can cause 
abortion, pre-term labour and dam age to the embryo.  It-could 
also affect the quality of the egg.

SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL: Children are the 
main prey to tobacco smoking. Maladies in children include 
asthma, bronchitis, pneumonia, lung cancer and irritation to 
eyes, nose and respiratory tract. Presence of toxic component 
of tobacco smoke has been shown by scientists in the hair, 
body fluid and tissues of non-smokers exposed to smoking. 
According to WHO, about half of the world's children are 
exposed to tobacco smoke by the adults who smoke. For 
young children, major source of tobacco smoke is their parents 
and other household members. Maternal smoking during 
pregnancy is one of the major causes of Sudden Infant Death 
Syndrome (SIDS), including low birth weight. Some of the 
reports show that  nasal cancer is associated with smoking. 
Madam, India is the world's third largest tobacco 
producing country. Nearly 50 per cent of the tobacco produced 
is consumed in the domestic market annually. In 1992, India 
produced about 767,436 million manufactured cigarettes and 
bidis, accounting for 13.5 per cent of the world's total. Of these, 
about 2,100 million cigarettes were exported. India's earnings 
from tobacco exports totalled at US $ 127.7 million. 
This seems to be the main consideration for India 
clearing a proposal to allow India Tobacco Corporation to triple 
the capacity of its Kidderpore Plant in Calcutta from 4.8 billion 
to 12.25 billion cigarettes. Similarly, the Government has 
allowed cent per cent FDI in India for the U.K. based 
Rothmans of Pall Mall International and to set up a new $ 150 
million plant. 
However, we must not forget that the revenue earned 
from the tobacco industry is far less than the expenditure 
incurred on patients suffering from tobacco-related diseases. 
261 

RAJYA   SABHA [24 November. 2000]  
While it is heartening that some States, including the 
National Capita! Territory of Delhi, are conscious of the 
hazards of smoking and have undertaken suitable legislation in 
this regard, their implementation is half-hearted, as indicated in 
a recent Press report. I quote: 
"In a startling revelation, it has come to light that at 
least 25 per cent of the persons challaned or fined for 
violating the provisions of Delhi Prohibition of Smoking 
Act in public transport buses and Government offices 
during the past two years were the ones supposed to 
ensure the enforcement of the same law. The offenders 
include employees who were found smoking within 
Government office premises or in the Delhi Transport 
Corporation buses and those running under the DTC's   
Kilometre Scheme." 
The contention that smoking causes disease is almost 
as old as the use of tobacco itself. One of the first published 
reports on the subject was issued in 1859; it showed that of 68 
patients in a hospital at Montpellier. France, who had cancer of 
the lips, tongue, tonsils or other parts of the mouth, used 
tobacco. 
It is imperative that the society should have healthy 
outlets. Some of the charges levelled against smoking are: 
(a) Smoking becomes an instrument for retract and 
withdrawal from 
society. It invariably rejects the values and life-styles of 
others along with at times being a visible means of 
dissent. Above all, it represents a new pleasure ethic 
that tries to break down the old work ethic. 
(b) Smokers seem to have a low level of tolerance in terms 
of anxiety and frustration. They are always eager to use 
props whenever they feel insecure. 
(c) It is said that smokers suffer from weak e;)o and super 
ego. They are unable to resolve their emotional and 
neurotic conflicts underlying in their psyche. 
We must try and combat the menace of smoking 
urgently. There is no time to lose. A firm Central legislation is 
the only remedy. A beginning can be made with prevention of 
smoking tobacco, in any form, at places of work and in public 
transport vehicles immediately 
The question was proposed.

LOWER TRADE GAP 
*101. SHRI K.C. KONDAIAH: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state; 
(a) whether it is a fact that during the first half of current financial year 
00-01 there has been noticeable lower tr ade gap as a result of increase in 
ort; 
(b) if so, the details thereof: and 
(c) the anticipated trade gap for whole financial year thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
.NDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a ) to (c) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The trade deficit for April-September, 2000-2001 is 
estimated at US $4673.51 million which is lower than the deficit at US $ 5012.88 
million during April-September, 1999-2000. 
(c) The export growth for the period April-September, 2000-2001 has been 
22.04% in US dollar terms over the corresponding period last year based on the 
latest provisional figures as provided by Directorate General of Commercial 
Intelligence & Statistics (DGCI&S), Calcutta, The target for export growth for 
the current year i.e. 2000-2001 is 18%. Imports are expected to be higher due 
to higher value of oil imports though non-oil imports have been lower by 
1.85% during April- September, 2000 over the corresponding period last year. 
The higher exports is expected to substantially compensate for the rise in 
import bill due to high oil prices.

Statement 
(a) and (b) Besides the on-going programmes being implemented by the State 
Governments for rehabilitation of person s with disabilities in the NER, this 
Ministry supports special education, vocational training, assessment and fitment of 
assistive devices, parent training and manpower development programmes being 
implemented by the National Institutes and NGOs for persons with disabilities in the 
NER. 17, 23 and 27 NGOs working for welfare of persons with disabilities have 
been provided financial assistance to the tune of Rs. 51.43 lakhs, 110.14 lakhs and 
179.82 lakhs in the years 1997-98, 1998-99 and 1999-2000 respectively. A 
number of new schemes are also being implemented by the Government for 
rehabilitation of persons with disabilities in the NER. 
These include—  
(i) National Programme for Rehabilitation of Persons with Disabilities 
(NPRPD)—approved as a state s ector scheme, under which Rs. 1 
crore was devolved to the 8 NER states in 1999-2000 for 
establishing the State Referral Centres for Rehabilitation of Persons 
with Disabilities. For 2000-2001, financial resources amounting to 
Rs. 1091.2 lakhs have been approved for covering 16 districts and its 
corresponding Blocks and Gram Panchayats along with continuing 
services at the State Referral Centres.

INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) and (b) The Committee on 
Agriculture of the World Trade Organisation has met in a Special session from

During the Special Session, proposals on "Non-trade Concerns' by 24 
member countries including European  Communities, Japan, Switzerland, 
Republic of Korea, Norway and some other developing countries, and least 
developed countries, and on "Export Subsidies, Food Security or Food

the fac    at though sufficient flexibility is required by large agrarian developing 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2000] 
economies to address their food and livelihood security concerns, it is not 
supportive of the attempts of certain developed countries to maintain their trade 
distorting subsidies under the garb of "multifunctionality'. India has supported the 
proposal on Export Subsidies, Food Security and Food Dependency as was put 
forward by Argentina and others. Philippines on behalf of Association of South 
East Asian Nations (ASEAN) introduced a paper on "Special and Differential 
Provisions which was supported by India in its intervention. Besides these, 2 other 
proposals on market access and domestic support were introduced by transition 
economies viz. Albania, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Georgia, Hungary, 
Kyrgyz Republic, Latvia, Lithuania, Mongolia, Slovak Republic, Slovenia, and

(c) and (d) India had earlier co-sponsored a paper on "Market access' along 
with 11 other developing countries during the Special session of the Committee on 
agriculture in the month of September 2000. In this paper trade distortions 
prevalent in international markets and the consequent hindrance to the exports 
from the develping countries have been highlighted and it has been proposed 
that developed countries should effect substantial reductions in their tariffs on a 
weighted average basis, eliminate tariff peaks and tariff escalations. It has also 
been demanded that the administration of tariff rate quotas (TRQs) should be 
made transparent and equitable for all trading partners, and there should be 
regular enhancement of TRQs so as to improve market access for all developing 
countries. All forms of trade distorting export subsidies must be eliminated by 
developed countries and domestic suppor t provided by developed countries 
should be substantially reduced, dumping must be prohibited and the provisions 
of the SPS Agreement which inhibit the ability of developing countries to export 
agricultural products should be suitably addressed.

Restructuring of HMT 
725. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have prepared some plans to restructure 
HMT; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof; and 
(c) whether it is also a fact that HMT is in the list of disinvestment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES (DR. VALLABHBHAI KATHIRIA): (a) to (c) 
Government has recently approved a turn  around plan for HMT. As per the 
turnaround plan, the three business groups of the company, i.e., Machine Tools, 
Watches and Tractors are to be disinvested upto 74% after their subsidiarisation. 
The process of subsidiarisation has already been initiated. 
The other salient features of the turnaround plan are as under:—  
(i) Government of India loan of Rs. 39.70 crores has been converted 
into equity and interest accrued thereon of Rs. 12.74 crore has been 
written off. 
(ii) Fresh equity of Rs. 250 crore has been provided. 
(iii) Notice for closure of five unviable units has been given and 
Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) extended to their 454 employees. 
(iv) Government has guaranteed issue of bonds by HMT to raise Rs. 
469 crore for funding VRS for retiring 6493 employees within 2 
years and provide interest subsidy of 50% along with guarantee 
fee waiver. 
(v) Watch Factory, Srinagar to be constituted as a subsidiary and be 
provided, for a period of three years, annual budgetary support to 
meet wages and salary outgo. 
(vi) Besides, Government has extended guarantee to avail of working 
capital loan for the Watch subsidiary and Rs. 15.10 crore for capital 
expenditure.

Statement-I 
Scheme for the welfare of handicapped in the country 
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is committed to provide equal 
opportunities, protection of rights full participation and all round development 
of persons with disabilities for achieving this goal, this Ministry runs various 
programmes / schemes. Important among them are:—  
1. In consonance with the policy of providing a complete package of 
welfare services to the physically, mentally, hearing and visually 
handicapped individuals and groups and in order to effectively 
deal with the multidimensional problems of the handicapped 
population, six National / Apex Institute each working in the specific 
area of disability, have been established. These Institutes are apex 
level organizations in the field of education, training, vocational 
guidance, counselling, research, rehabilitation and development of 
suitable service modules for the disabled. 
2 A National Trust for the Welfare of  Persons with Autism, Cerebral 
Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities has been created 
to provide support to these vulner able categories of disabled and 
their families.

3. To suport entrepreneurial activities by the persons with disabilities, 
the National Handicapped Finance and Development Corporation 
has been set up as an apex level financial institution for routing 
funds through the channelising agen cies authorized by the State / 
UT Governments. The main objective of the Corporation is to provide 
self-employment and income generating activities to persons with 
disabilities for their economic rehabilitation. 
4. The Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation (ALIMCO), 
Kanpur was establihsed in November, 1972 as a Public Sector 
Company with the main objective of developing and manufactur-
ing standard aids and appliances for the disabled persons and to 
make them available at reasonable prices to them throughout India. 
It manufacturers wheel chairs, tricyc le, artificial limbs, crutches 
and may other aids and appliances for the handicapped persons. A 
scheme for setting up for Auxiliary Production Centres of ALIMCO 
has been launched recently with a view to expand the production 
base of ALIMCO. 
5. Two Schemes, namely, (a) Scheme to Promote Voluntary Action 
for Persons with Disabilities and (b) Scheme of Assistance to 
Disabted Persons for purchase / fitting of aids and appliances 
(ADIP) are being implemented for providing support to non-
governmental agencies working for various programmes for 
rehabilitation of persons with disabilities. 
6. Under the Scheme of Employment of the Handicapped, financial 
assistance is provide to States/ UT Administrations for running 
special employment exchanges and for operating special cells in 
normal employment exchanges for persons with disabilities. 
7. A Central Scheme for Sitting up of five Composite resoure Centres 
(CRCs) have been approved with the objecive of creating an 
infrastructure for serving as composite outreach extension centres 
of the National Institutes. 
8. The District Rehabilitation Centre Schme (DRC) was initiated by 
the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment to provide 
comprehensive rehabilitation services to the rural disabled right at 
"their doorstep in 11 district of the country. Four Regional

provided by DDA, a preliminary inquiry was conducted into reports/complaints 
of irregularities in the restoration/allotment of flats, which prima-facie revealed

allotment of SFS flats, and also in respect of refunds in some cases. On the basis

of Delhi Police for further investigation.

already placed under suspension earlier. The remaining 6 officials have also since 
been placed under suspension. The case is being investigated by CBI. 
DDA have reported that they have taken several steps to streamline the procedure so 
that no wrong restoration/refund take place these include: the system of restoring the 
cases through the Grievances Redressal Committee has been discontinued and in the 
future each case will considered on merits on each individual file so that proper 
accountability can be ensured; where there is any reduction in the cost of flat or in the 
fifth and final demand letter, prior approval of Commissioner (Housing) would be

Slow Implementation of Poverty Alleviation Programmes 
† 807. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that poverty  alleviation programmes are being 
implemented very slow; 
(b) if so, whether Government are considering to take certain concrete steps 
to accelerate the same; and 
(c) if so, the outline thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) to (c) This Minist ry has been implementing an Urban 
Poverty Alleviation Programme called Swarna Jayanti Sahari Rojgar Yojana 
(SJSRY) w.e.f. 1.12.97. 
The performance under SJSRY has been relatively low, since it is a new 
scheme. Moreover, the States/UTs took some time to conduct fresh surveys for 
identifying target groups and to train the concerned Staff. There was also a 
backlog of unutilised funds from the earlier UPA schemes. 
However, the programme is being monitored vigorously through quarterly 
progress reports, periodica! review meetings at the level of Minister/Secretary 
with the concerned Secretaries of the State/UT Governments and through field 
visits by the officers of this Ministry. In view of these steps, an improvement in 
the implementation of the scheme is anticipated. 
Green Hyderabad Project 
808. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMCHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the State Government of Andhra Pradesh has launched a Green 
Hyderabad Project with Dutch assistance; 
(b) if so, the main points of the project; 
(c) the total financial outlay of this project; 
(d) the total amount to be provided by the Dutch Government in the 
implementation of the project; and 
(e) by when the work on this project is likely to start?  
† Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [27 November, 2000] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) The Green Hyderabad Project has not been launched by 
the Government of Andhra Pradesh. A draft Project Report titled Green 
Hyderabad Project 2000— 2005 prepared  by Hyderabad Urban Development 
Authority was sent to the Royal Netherlands Embassy (RNE). Royal Netherlands 
Embassy had sent a Mission to appraise the project. Based on its 
recommendations another Mission was sent by RNE for project formulation. 
The Formulation Mission had given its report to Hyderabad Urban Development 
Authority. These proposals will be forwarded to the RNE for aid through 
Government of India. The Royal Netherlands Embassy has agreed to consider 
this proposal in principle. 
(b) The main components of the project proposal are: 
(i) Creation and Conservation of Greenery covering an area of 12,100 
hectares. 
(ii) Integrate lake treatment and conservation covering an area of 1,300 
hectares. 
(iii) Support activity like training, awareness campaigns, valuation along 
with necessary infrastructure like staff/vehicles etc. for successful 
implementation of the project. 
(c) and (d) The total financial outlay of the project proposal as per Formulation 
Mission Report is Rs. 159.69 crores, out of which Rs. 127.75 crores is proposed 
as grant from the Royal Netherlands Government, Rs. 22.03 crores as contribution 
from implementing agencies/Government of Andhra Pradesh and Rs. 9.92 as 
contribution from community and private participation. 
(e) The project is likely to start from 01.04.2001, subject to Government of 
India entering into agreement with the Royal Netherlands Government.

It is a well-known fact that the world-famous Kohinoor 
diamond belonged to India from time immemorial, though it passed 
under different names at different times. In the middle ages, it was 
Sultan Alauddin Khilji who took it away from the Hindu King of Malwa. 
But the Hindu Raja of Gwalior got it back. With the Mughal invasion, 
Badshah Babar acquired it; and till the decline of his dynasty, it was 
preserved by his successors as their preciousmost gem. In the year 
1739, the Persian invader, Nadir Shah, took away the diamond by 
trick from the defeated Mughal Emperor, Mohammad Shah. Nadir 
Shah gave the diamond a new name, that is, Kohinoor or the 
Mountain of Light. After Nadir's death, the King of Kabul captured the 
diamond. But it was Maharaja Ranjit Singh of Punjab who finally took 
possession of the Kohinoor from the Afghans. When the British 
conquered Punjab, they acquired it from King Dilip Singh, son of 
Maharaja Ranjit Singh. The Governor-General of the time sent it 
forthwith to Oueen Victoria; and till now the diamond is in Britain.
